notes.text: Profit-based, so negative on the b1_disclosure_principle: as gold rises, profit rises faster than revenue and the State's share rises with it. Same structural category as the NT. Two features distinguish it. (1) The escalator is BOUNDED — 1.9% floor to a hard 5.35% cap, a 2.8x slope that stops rather than compounding indefinitely, which makes it strictly better than an uncapped profit regime. (2) Prior-year losses are NOT carried forward, so the profit component re-engages immediately after a downturn rather than being sheltered by accumulated losses. That is adverse precisely in a recovery off a gold trough — the leg of the cycle this index is built to capture. The 20% in-State metal-production rebate is unlikely to apply to a doré producer shipping to a mainland refiner. Compare Queensland, verified the same day: also a bounded escalator, but one already at its ceiling, so Queensland's convexity is spent and Tasmania's is live between 1.9% and 5.35%.

title: Public Ruling MRA002.3 Determination of royalty for prescribed and specified minerals - Queensland Revenue Office
tier_note: revenue authority publishing statutory royalty rates in its mandate

notes.text: THE BLOCKING QUESTION IS ANSWERED, AND THE ANSWER IS NOT THE ONE THE QUESTION EXPECTED. Queensland does run gold on a price-linked sliding scale — exactly the call-spread mechanism B1 exists to find — but the escalator is CAPPED at 5% and has been SATURATED for two decades. Reference price 2 is A$890/oz; spot on the 18 Aug 2026 build is A$6,216/oz, seven times it. Public Ruling MRA002.3's own worked gold example applies '5% for gold' for the December 2020 quarter, when gold was around US$1,800-1,920/oz. So: the marginal convexity of the Queensland gold royalty at any price this index cares about is EXACTLY ZERO. Above A$890/oz the regime is a flat 5% ad valorem and behaves identically to WA's flat 2.5% — at double the rate. All of the negative convexity was realised between A$600 and A$890/oz, long before the index existed. Two consequences worth stating plainly. First, a scoring rule that 'penalised in proportion to the escalator's slope' — a rule no code ever implemented — would have penalised Queensland for a slope of zero, and would have been WRONG in the direction it was most confident about. That is a good argument for treating it as disclosure rather than a score. Second, the risk that remains is not convexity: it is that A$890 and 5% are numbers in a regulation, the regulation was remade as recently as 1 September 2025, and Queensland has form on resource royalties (the 2022 coal tiers). A cap is only as good as the statute holding it. Also note there is NO processing discount for gold or silver, unlike the other prescribed minerals.

tier_note: state minerals regulator

notes.text: §2.3's prose asserted 'flat ad valorem' before the data supported it — this file carried rate null, convexity 'presumed neutral', verified false while the methodology stated the conclusion. CONFIRMED, not corrected: the structure is flat and no price-linked element applies to gold. The rate is 4.0%, 1.6x Western Australia. The base is 'ex-mine value' — the value of the mineral once mined and brought to the surface — with deductions confined to the direct costs of upgrading and bringing material to market after the first stockpile, so the base is narrower than a gross-revenue base and the two rates are not perfectly comparable. Gold is a publicly owned mineral in NSW, so the whole royalty accrues to the state; for privately owned minerals seven-eighths is returned to the owner. Contrast NSW's flat 4% with Queensland's escalator: the state that took the intervention event has the more predictable fiscal claim.

title: Royalties | Mineral Resources Tasmania
tier_note: state minerals regulator

notes.text: Profit-based, so negative on the b1_disclosure_principle: as gold rises, profit rises faster than revenue and the State's share rises with it. Same structural category as the NT. Two features distinguish it. (1) The escalator is BOUNDED — 1.9% floor to a hard 5.35% cap, a 2.8x slope that stops rather than compounding indefinitely, which makes it strictly better than an uncapped profit regime. (2) Prior-year losses are NOT carried forward, so the profit component re-engages immediately after a downturn rather than being sheltered by accumulated losses. That is adverse precisely in a recovery off a gold trough — the leg of the cycle this index is built to capture. The 20% in-State metal-production rebate is unlikely to apply to a doré producer shipping to a mainland refiner. Compare Queensland, verified the same day: also a bounded escalator, but one already at its ceiling, so Queensland's convexity is spent and Tasmania's is live between 1.9% and 5.35%.

title: Mineral royalty rates - Queensland Revenue Office
tier_note: revenue authority publishing statutory royalty rates in its mandate

notes.text: THE BLOCKING QUESTION IS ANSWERED, AND THE ANSWER IS NOT THE ONE THE QUESTION EXPECTED. Queensland does run gold on a price-linked sliding scale — exactly the call-spread mechanism B1 exists to find — but the escalator is CAPPED at 5% and has been SATURATED for two decades. Reference price 2 is A$890/oz; spot on the 18 Aug 2026 build is A$6,216/oz, seven times it. Public Ruling MRA002.3's own worked gold example applies '5% for gold' for the December 2020 quarter, when gold was around US$1,800-1,920/oz. So: the marginal convexity of the Queensland gold royalty at any price this index cares about is EXACTLY ZERO. Above A$890/oz the regime is a flat 5% ad valorem and behaves identically to WA's flat 2.5% — at double the rate. All of the negative convexity was realised between A$600 and A$890/oz, long before the index existed. Two consequences worth stating plainly. First, a scoring rule that 'penalised in proportion to the escalator's slope' — a rule no code ever implemented — would have penalised Queensland for a slope of zero, and would have been WRONG in the direction it was most confident about. That is a good argument for treating it as disclosure rather than a score. Second, the risk that remains is not convexity: it is that A$890 and 5% are numbers in a regulation, the regulation was remade as recently as 1 September 2025, and Queensland has form on resource royalties (the 2022 coal tiers). A cap is only as good as the statute holding it. Also note there is NO processing discount for gold or silver, unlike the other prescribed minerals.
